results.title: Partition of a group
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a group. A set $C$ of subgroups of $G$ is a partition of $G$ when every member of $C$ is a proper subgroup of $G$, every element of $G$ lies in some member of $C$, and any two distinct members of $C$ intersect in the trivial subgroup. The members of $C$ are called its components.

results.title: Separability in the class of finite $p$-groups

results.title: Arboricity colorings
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph and $k$ a natural number. A labeling of the edges of $G$ with labels in $\{0, 1, \dots, k - 1\}$ is an arboricity coloring when, for each label $i$, the graph on the vertices of $G$ whose edges are the edges of $G$ labeled $i$ is acyclic, that is, a forest.

results.title: Nash–Williams arboricity theorem
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $G$ be a simple graph on a finite vertex set $V$ and let $k$ be a natural number. Then $G$ has an arboricity coloring with $k$ labels, that is, its edges can be labeled with $k$ labels so that the edges of each label form a forest, if and only if for every nonempty set $U \subseteq V$, the number of edges of $G$ with both endpoints in $U$ is at most $k(|U| - 1)$.

results.title: Graph of a PARTITION INTO PATHS OF LENGTH 2 instance

Pairs in $E$ with an entry at least $n$, and pairs $(u, u)$, contribute no edge.

results.title: Well-formed PARTITION INTO PATHS OF LENGTH 2 instances

results.title: Partitions into paths of length 2

results.title: PARTITION INTO PATHS OF LENGTH 2

results.summary: The decision problem PARTITION INTO PATHS OF LENGTH 2 accepts a bitstring $x$ exactly when $x$ decodes, under the canonical bitstring encoding of instances, to an instance $(n, E)$ that is well formed and admits a partition into paths of length 2. results.title: Büchi acceptance condition
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A nondeterministic Büchi automaton accepts an infinite word $x = x_0 x_1 x_2 \cdots$ if and only if it has a run on $x$, that is, a sequence of states $s_0 s_1 s_2 \cdots$ with $s_0$ a start state and a transition from $s_k$ to $s_{k+1}$ reading $x_k$ for every $k$, such that $s_k$ is an accepting state for infinitely many $k$.

results.title: Lassos give accepted ultimately periodic words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $\mathcal{A}$ be a nondeterministic Büchi automaton over a nonempty alphabet. Suppose $s_0$ is a start state and $s$ an accepting state of $\mathcal{A}$, that reading the finite word $u$ the automaton can move from $s_0$ to $s$, and that reading a nonempty finite word $v$ it can move from $s$ back to $s$. Then $\mathcal{A}$ accepts the infinite word $u v^\omega = u v v v \cdots$.

results.title: An accepted word yields a lasso
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states accepts some infinite word, then it has a lasso: some accepting state is visited twice along an accepting run, and the run between the two visits is the cycle.

results.title: Lasso characterization of Büchi nonemptiness
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For finitely many states, the language of a nondeterministic Büchi automaton is nonempty iff some accepting state is reachable from a start state and lies on a nonempty cycle.

results.title: Nonempty Büchi languages contain ultimately periodic words
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states over a nonempty alphabet. If $A$ accepts some infinite word, then there are finite words $u$ and $v$ with $v$ nonempty such that $A$ accepts the ultimately periodic word $u v^\omega = u v v v \cdots$.

results.title: Reachability by words is reachability in the transition graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For states $s$ and $t$ of a nondeterministic Büchi automaton, the automaton can move from $s$ to $t$ by reading some finite word (possibly empty) if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in zero or more steps of the transition graph, which has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

results.title: Nonempty words and paths of positive length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For states $s$ and $t$ of a nondeterministic Büchi automaton, the automaton can move from $s$ to $t$ by reading some nonempty finite word if and only if $t$ is reachable from $s$ in one or more steps of the transition graph, which has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

results.title: The lasso condition in the transition graph
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: A nondeterministic Büchi automaton has a lasso if and only if there are a start state $s_0$ and an accepting state $s$ such that $s$ is reachable from $s_0$ in zero or more steps of the transition graph and $s$ is reachable from itself in one or more steps; the transition graph has an edge from $p$ to $q$ when some symbol takes $p$ to $q$.

results.title: Finite set of start states
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and a decidable start set, this is the set of its start states, viewed as a finite set.

results.title: Lasso states of a finite Büchi automaton
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states, decidable equality of states, a finite alphabet, and decidable transitions, start set and accepting set, the lasso states form the finite set of accepting states $s$ that are reachable from some start state in zero or more transitions and lie on a nonempty cycle, that is, $s$ is reachable from itself in one or more transitions.

results.title: Lasso detection by finite reachability
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $A$ be a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable. Then $A$ has a lasso if and only if its set of lasso states, computed by finite reachability closures as the accepting states that are reachable from a start state and lie on a nonempty cycle, is nonempty.

results.title: Büchi emptiness test
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable, the emptiness test returns true exactly when the automaton has no lasso. It decides this by computing the set of lasso states; by the lasso characterization, it returns true iff no infinite word is accepted.

results.title: Correctness of the Büchi emptiness test
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a nondeterministic Büchi automaton with finitely many states and finitely many symbols, with decidable equality of states, and whose transitions, start states and accepting states are decidable, the emptiness test returns true if and only if the automaton accepts no infinite word.

results.title: Range tree
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: A one-dimensional range tree over the integers is either empty, a single leaf holding an integer, or a binary node made of two integers $l$ and $h$ together with a left and a right subtree. The integers $l$ and $h$ are meant to cache the interval $[l, h]$ spanned by the leaf values of the node's subtree; the type does not enforce this, the bounds-correctness predicate does.

results.title: Leaf traversal of a range tree with an accumulator
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a range tree $t$ and a list $a$ of integers, $\operatorname{aux}(t, a)$ is $a$ if $t$ is empty, the list $x$ followed by $a$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and $\operatorname{aux}(L, \operatorname{aux}(R, a))$ if $t$ is a node with left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$.

results.title: Leaf list of a range tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The leaf list of a range tree $t$ is the list of the integers stored at its leaves, read from left to right and with repetitions.

results.title: Range-tree leaf traversal appends to its accumulator
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every range tree $t$ and every list $a$ of integers, the accumulator leaf traversal of $t$ started from $a$ equals the leaf list of $t$ followed by $a$.

results.title: Leaf list of a range-tree node
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For all integers $lo$, $hi$ and range trees $L$, $R$, the leaf list of the node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$, left subtree $L$ and right subtree $R$ is the leaf list of $L$ followed by the leaf list of $R$.

results.title: Number of leaves of a range tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The size of a range tree is its number of leaves: $0$ for the empty tree, $1$ for a leaf, and the sum of the sizes of the two children for a node.

results.title: Length of the leaf list of a range tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every range tree $t$, the list of leaf values of $t$ read from left to right has length equal to the number of leaves of $t$.

results.title: Cached lower bound of a range tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a range tree $t$, $\operatorname{tmin}(t)$ is $0$ if $t$ is empty, $x$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and the stored lower bound $lo$ if $t$ is a node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$ and two subtrees.

results.title: Cached upper bound of a range tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a range tree $t$, $\operatorname{tmax}(t)$ is $0$ if $t$ is empty, $x$ if $t$ is a single leaf with value $x$, and the stored upper bound $hi$ if $t$ is a node with stored bounds $lo$, $hi$ and two subtrees.

results.title: Bounds-valid range trees
results.caption: Inductive
results.summary: For a range tree $s$, write $s_{\min}$ and $s_{\max}$ for its cached lower and upper bounds: the stored interval endpoints at a node, the value itself at a leaf, and $0$ for the empty tree. Bounds-validity is defined inductively: the empty tree and every leaf are bounds-valid, and a node with cached interval $[a, b]$, left child $\ell$ and right child $r$ is bounds-valid when $\ell$ and $r$ are bounds-valid, each…

results.title: Valid range tree
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: A range tree $t$ is valid when it has correct cached bounds (every node has two subtrees with nonempty leaf lists, and its stored lower and upper bounds are the minimum of the lower bounds and the maximum of the upper bounds of its two subtrees, recursively) and its leaf list is sorted in nondecreasing order.

results.title: Valid range trees have sorted leaves
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: If a range tree $t$ is valid, then its list of leaf values, read from left to right, is sorted in nondecreasing order.

results.title: Leaf values of a bounds-valid tree lie between the cached bounds
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree, and write $t_{\min}$ and $t_{\max}$ for its cached lower and upper bounds. Then every leaf value $x$ of $t$ satisfies $t_{\min} \le x \le t_{\max}$.

results.title: The cached bounds of a nonempty bounds-valid range tree are leaf values
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree with at least one leaf. Then the cached lower bound of $t$ and the cached upper bound of $t$ are both leaf values of $t$.

results.title: Accumulator range report
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For integers $a$, $b$ and a list $\mathit{acc}$ of integers, the accumulator range report of a range tree for $[a, b]$ starting from $\mathit{acc}$ is defined by recursion on the tree. The empty tree returns $\mathit{acc}$. A leaf with value $x$ returns $x$ followed by $\mathit{acc}$ if $a \le x \le b$, and $\mathit{acc}$ otherwise. A node with cached interval $[l, h]$ returns $\mathit{acc}$ if $h < a$ or $b < l$;…

results.title: Range report
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The range report of a range tree $t$ for integers $a$ and $b$ is the accumulator range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ starting from the empty list.

results.title: Accumulator range report of a bounds-valid range tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree, let $a$ and $b$ be integers and let $\mathit{acc}$ be a list of integers. Then the accumulator range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ starting from $\mathit{acc}$ is the list of the leaf values $x$ of $t$ with $a \le x \le b$, in left-to-right order and with repetitions, followed by $\mathit{acc}$.

results.title: Correctness of the range report
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a range tree satisfying the bounds-correctness predicate: every node has two subtrees with at least one leaf each and caches the least and the greatest leaf value of its subtree. For all integers $a$ and $b$, the range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ equals the list of leaf values $x$ of $t$ with $a \le x \le b$, in left-to-right order.

results.title: Membership in a range report
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a range tree satisfying the bounds-correctness predicate: every node has two subtrees with at least one leaf each and caches the least and the greatest leaf value of its subtree. For all integers $a$, $b$ and $x$, the value $x$ occurs in the range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$ if and only if $x$ is a leaf value of $t$ and $a \le x \le b$.

results.title: Range count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a range tree $t$ and integers $a$ and $b$, the range count of $t$ over $[a, b]$ is the length of the range report of $t$ for $[a, b]$.

results.title: Range count of a bounds-valid tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $t$ be a bounds-valid range tree and let $a$ and $b$ be integers. Then the range count of $t$ over $[a, b]$ equals the number of leaves of $t$ whose value lies in $[a, b]$.

results.title: Building a range tree from a list
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a range tree $s$, write $s_{\min}$ and $s_{\max}$ for its cached lower and upper bounds. The range tree built from a list $L$ of integers of length $n$ is defined by recursion on $n$: the empty list gives the empty tree, a one-element list $[x]$ gives the leaf $x$, and for $n \ge 2$ it is the node whose left child $\ell$ is the tree built from the first $\lfloor n/2 \rfloor$ entries of $L$, whose right child…

results.title: Building a range tree preserves the list
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ of integers, the leaf list of the range tree built from $xs$ is $xs$.

results.title: Size of a built range tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $\mathit{xs}$ of integers, the range tree built from $\mathit{xs}$ has exactly as many leaves as $\mathit{xs}$ has elements.

results.title: Built range trees are bounds-valid
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ of integers, the range tree built from $L$ by recursive halving is bounds-valid.

results.title: Building from a sorted list gives a valid range tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $xs$ of integers that is sorted in nondecreasing order, the range tree built from $xs$ is valid.

results.title: Range report on a built tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $\mathit{xs}$ of integers and all integers $a$ and $b$, the range report for $[a, b]$ on the range tree built from $\mathit{xs}$ equals the list of elements $x$ of $\mathit{xs}$ with $a \le x \le b$, in their original order.

results.title: Range counting on a built tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ of integers and all integers $a$ and $b$, the range count over $[a, b]$ of the range tree built from $L$ equals the number of entries of $L$, counted with multiplicity, that lie in $[a, b]$.

results.title: Range report membership on a built tree
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every list $L$ of integers and all integers $a$, $b$ and $x$, the value $x$ occurs in the range report for $[a, b]$ on the range tree built from $L$ if and only if $x$ is an entry of $L$ and $a \le x \le b$.

results.title: Discrete Fourier sum
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $N$, a complex number $\omega$, a sequence $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and a natural number $k$, the unnormalized discrete Fourier sum of length $N$ at frequency $k$ is $\sum_{j=0}^{N-1} \omega^{jk} f(j)$.

results.title: Even–odd splitting of the DFT sum
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $n$, every $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$, every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $K$,

results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy $\omega^n = 1$. Then for every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $K$, the discrete Fourier sum of length $n$ at frequency $K$ equals the one at frequency $K \bmod n$:

results.title: Radix-2 Cooley–Tukey splitting
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$, $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and natural numbers $N$ and $k$, write $D_N(\omega, f, k) = \sum_{j < N} \omega^{jk} f(j)$ for the discrete Fourier sum. Let $n$ be a natural number and let $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ satisfy $\omega^{2n} = 1$. Then for every $f : \mathbb{N} \to \mathbb{C}$ and every natural number $K$,

results.title: FFT operation count
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a natural number $n$, the closed-form FFT operation count is $n \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$, where $\lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ is the largest $m$ with $2^m \le n$ (taken to be $0$ when $n = 0$).

results.title: The FFT cost satisfies the radix-2 recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $C(n) = n \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ be the closed-form FFT operation count. For every natural number $n > 0$, $C(2n) = 2\,C(n) + 2n$.

results.title: Even–odd split for the FFT
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, a natural number $m$ and a vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1}) \in R^{2m}$, the split returns the pair of vectors $(x_0, x_2, \dots, x_{2m-2})$ and $(x_1, x_3, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ in $R^m$ of the entries of $x$ at even and at odd indices, in order, at a time cost of $4m$ (the charged reads and writes).

results.title: One FFT butterfly
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\omega \in R$, vectors $q, r \in R^m$, a state $(w, y)$ with $w \in R$ and $y \in R^{2m}$, and an index $k < m$, the butterfly at $k$ returns the state $(w \omega, y')$, where $y'$ is obtained from $y$ by setting entry $k$ to $q_k + w r_k$ and entry $k + m$ to $q_k - w r_k$, at a time cost of $8$.

results.title: FFT butterfly pass
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, an element $\omega \in R$ and vectors $q, r \in R^m$ and $y \in R^{2m}$, the butterfly pass starts from the state $(1, y)$, applies the FFT butterfly with $\omega$, $q$ and $r$ at the indices $k = 0, 1, \dots, m - 1$ in increasing order, and returns the final state; its time cost is the sum of the costs of these $m$ butterflies.

results.title: Radix-two fast Fourier transform
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: For a commutative ring $R$, a natural number $d$, an element $\omega \in R$ and a vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ is defined by recursion on $d$. For $d = 0$ it returns $x$ at cost $0$. For $d + 1$ it splits $x$ into its even- and odd-indexed subvectors $e, o \in R^{2^d}$ (cost $4 \cdot 2^d$), computes $\omega^2$ (cost $1$), computes the FFTs $q$ of $e$ and $r$ of $o$ with root $\omega^2$,…

results.title: Radix-two FFT on arrays
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ an array over $R$ of length $n$, and let $d = \lfloor \log_2 n \rfloor$ (with $d = 0$ when $n = 0$). If $n = 2^d$, the array FFT runs the radix-two FFT with root $\omega$ on $x$, viewed as a vector of length $2^d$, and returns its output as an array, with the cost of that run. Otherwise it returns no result, at cost $0$; the length check itself is free.

results.title: The array FFT rejects exactly the non-powers of two
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ an array over $R$. The array FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ returns no result if and only if the length of $x$ is different from $2^d$ for every natural number $d$.

results.title: Lower write of a butterfly step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state $(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $k$ is $q_k + w r_k$.

results.title: Upper write of a butterfly step
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state $(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $k + m$ is $q_k - w r_k$.

results.title: A butterfly step leaves other entries unchanged
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q, r$ vectors over $R$ of length $m$, $w \in R$ a twiddle, $o$ an output vector over $R$ of length $2m$, and $k < m$. Then for every index $i < 2m$ with $i \ne k$ and $i \ne k + m$, the butterfly step at index $k$ applied to the state $(w, o)$ produces an output vector whose entry at index $i$ is $o_i$.

results.title: Result of the butterfly loop
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $\omega \in R$, $m$ a natural number, $q = (q_0, \dots, q_{m-1})$ and $r = (r_0, \dots, r_{m-1})$ vectors over $R$, and $o$ a vector over $R$ of length $2m$. The butterfly loop with root $\omega$ on $q$ and $r$, started from twiddle $1$ and output vector $o$, ends with twiddle $\omega^m$ and an output vector $y$ such that $y_k = q_k + \omega^k r_k$ and $y_{k+m} = q_k - \omega^k r_k$…

results.title: The FFT split extracts the even-indexed entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a type, $m$ a natural number and $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ a vector of length $2m$ over $R$. For every $k < m$, entry $k$ of the first (even) vector returned by the FFT split of $x$ is $x_{2k}$.

results.title: The FFT split extracts the odd-indexed entries
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a type, $m$ a natural number and $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2m-1})$ a vector of length $2m$ over $R$. For every $k < m$, entry $k$ of the second (odd) vector returned by the FFT split of $x$ is $x_{2k+1}$.

results.title: The FFT of depth zero returns its input
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^0}$, the vector returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $0$ with root $\omega$ on $x$ is $x$ itself.

results.title: Low half of the FFT butterfly recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x \in R^{2^{d+1}}$, with entries indexed from $0$. Let $e, o \in R^{2^d}$ be the even- and odd-indexed subsequences of $x$ returned by the FFT split, and let $E$ and $O$ be the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d$ with root $\omega \cdot \omega$ on $e$ and on $o$. Then for every $k < 2^d$, entry $k$ of the vector returned by the…

results.title: High half of the FFT butterfly recurrence
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x \in R^{2^{d+1}}$, with entries indexed from $0$. Let $e, o \in R^{2^d}$ be the even- and odd-indexed subsequences of $x$ returned by the FFT split, and let $E$ and $O$ be the vectors returned by the radix-two FFT of depth $d$ with root $\omega \cdot \omega$ on $e$ and on $o$. Then for every $k < 2^d$, entry $k + 2^d$ of the vector returned…

results.title: Cost of the FFT even/odd split
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $m$ and every vector $x$ of length $2m$, splitting $x$ into its even-indexed and its odd-indexed subsequences costs exactly $4m$ charged operations: two reads and two writes for each of the $m$ even/odd pairs.

results.title: Cost of one FFT butterfly
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m$ a natural number. For every $\omega \in R$, all vectors $q, r \in R^m$, every current twiddle $w \in R$ and output vector of length $2m$ over $R$, and every index $k < m$, one butterfly step costs exactly $8$ charged operations: two reads, four scalar operations and two writes.

results.title: Cost of the FFT butterfly pass
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring and $m$ a natural number. For every $\omega \in R$, all vectors $q, r \in R^m$ and every output vector of length $2m$ over $R$, the pass that, starting from twiddle $1$, applies one butterfly for each index $k < m$ in increasing order costs exactly $8m$ charged operations.

results.title: Exact cost of the radix-two FFT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number $d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ costs $T$ charged operations, where $T + 1 = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d$; that is, $T = (7d + 1) \cdot 2^d - 1$.

results.title: Exact cost of the radix-two FFT in terms of the input length
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number $d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x$ over $R$ of length $n = 2^d$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ costs $T$ charged operations, where $T + 1 = (7 \log_2 n + 1) \cdot n$.

results.title: Cost bound for the radix-two FFT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring. For every natural number $d$, every $\omega \in R$ and every vector $x \in R^{2^d}$, the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ costs at most $8 \cdot 2^d \cdot d$ charged operations, that is, at most eight per entry per recursion level.

results.title: Correctness of the radix-two FFT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For every natural number $d$, every primitive $2^d$-th root of unity $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$, every vector $x = (x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1})$ in $\mathbb{C}^{2^d}$ and every $k < 2^d$, the $k$-th entry of the radix-two FFT of $x$ with root $\omega$ equals the discrete Fourier sum $\sum_{j=0}^{2^d - 1} \omega^{jk} x_j$.

results.title: The array FFT agrees with the vector FFT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the array FFT of $x$, viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ returns a result, namely the output of the radix-two FFT of the length-$2^d$ vector $x$ with root $\omega$, viewed as an array.

results.title: The array FFT costs the same as the vector FFT
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $R$ be a commutative ring, $d$ a natural number, $\omega \in R$ and $x$ a vector over $R$ of length $2^d$. Then the cost of the array FFT of $x$, viewed as an array, with root $\omega$ equals the cost of the radix-two FFT of the length-$2^d$ vector $x$ with root $\omega$.

results.title: The array FFT computes the discrete Fourier transform
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Let $d$ be a natural number, $\omega \in \mathbb{C}$ a primitive $2^d$-th root of unity, $x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1}$ complex numbers and $k < 2^d$. Then the array FFT of the array $(x_0, \dots, x_{2^d - 1})$ with root $\omega$ returns an array $y$ of length $2^d$ whose entry at index $k$ is the discrete Fourier sum $\sum_{j=0}^{2^d - 1} \omega^{jk} x_j$.

results.title: Exact cost of the array FFT

results.title: Complementary base pairing of two positions
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Positions `i` and `j` of `s` both lie in `s` and carry complementary bases.

results.title: Inside recursion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Inside recursion over a commutative semiring `R`: `inside pair m s w i len` is the weighted sum over the secondary structures supported in the interval `[i, i + len)` (proved in `inside_eq_sum`). results.title: Outside recursion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Outside recursion (McCaskill 1990) over a commutative semiring `R`, for a sequence of length `n = s.length`: `outside pair m s w i j` is the weighted sum of the parts outside the pair `(i, j)` of all structures containing it (proved in `outside_mul_eq_sum`). Either no pair encloses `(i, j)`, leaving independent structures on `[0, i)` and `[j + 1, n)`, or there is a unique innermost enclosing pair `(a, b)` (`a < i`,…

results.title: Secondary structures within an interval
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The secondary structures on `s` (`IsStructure pair m s`) all of whose pairs lie in the interval `[i, i + len)`.

results.title: Set of all secondary structures of a sequence
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: All secondary structures on `s` with minimum hairpin `m` (see `mem_structures`).

results.title: Weight of a secondary structure
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The weight of a structure: the product of the weights of its base pairs.

results.title: Membership in the set of secondary structures
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: `structures` is exactly the set of secondary structures on `s`.

results.title: Inside algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The inside recursion sums the weights of all secondary structures supported in the interval `[i, i + len)`, over any commutative semiring.

results.title: Inside value sums the weights of all secondary structures
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The inside value of the whole sequence sums the weights of all its secondary structures.

results.title: Outside algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Outside algorithm (McCaskill 1990): for a candidate pair `(i, j)` (`i + m < j` and `CanPair pair s i j`), the outside value times the pair's weight times the inside value of the enclosed interval `[i + 1, j)` sums the weights of all secondary structures containing `(i, j)`.

results.title: Tropical semiring
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: With every base pair weighted `-1` in the min-plus semiring `MinTropical (WithTop ℤ)` (addition `min`, multiplication `+`), a structure with `k` pairs has weight `-k`, so the inside value of the whole sequence is minus the Nussinov maximum number of base pairs.

results.title: Waterman's recursion
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: Waterman's recursion for the number `S_m(n)` of secondary structures on `n` points with minimum hairpin `m` when every pair is allowed: `S(0) = 1` and `S(n + 1) = S(n) + ∑_{m ≤ k < n} S(k) S(n - 1 - k)` (Waterman 1978; Stein–Waterman 1979). For `m = 0` these are the Motzkin numbers (`watermanNumber_zero_eq_motzkinNumber`); for `m = 1` the Stein–Waterman numbers `1, 1, 1, 2, 4, 8, 17, 37, …` (OEIS A004148).

results.title: Counting semiring
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: The number of secondary structures on `n` points with minimum hairpin `m`, when every pair of positions may pair, is Waterman's number `S_m(n)`.

results.title: Waterman numbers with no hairpin constraint are Motzkin numbers
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For `m = 0` (no hairpin constraint) Waterman's numbers are the Motzkin numbers `M(n) = ∑_k C(n, 2k) C(k)`: the number of non-crossing partial matchings on `n` points.

results.title: Additive base-pair energy model
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: An additive base-pair energy model: the free energy of a structure is the sum of the energies `e i j` of its base pairs (in the same units as `RT`).

results.title: McCaskill partition function of RNA secondary structures
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The partition function `Z = ∑_S exp (-E(S) / RT)` over all secondary structures `S` on `s` with minimum hairpin `m`, for the additive energy `e` at thermal energy `RT` (physically `0 < RT`; the identities below hold for every real `RT`).

results.title: McCaskill's algorithm
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: McCaskill's algorithm (inside part): over the sum-product semiring `ℝ` with Boltzmann weights `exp (-e i j / RT)`, the inside value of the whole sequence is the partition function. This is an algebraic identity valid for every real `RT`.

results.title: Base-pair probability
results.caption: Definition
results.summary: The base-pair probability `P(i, j)`: the total weight of the structures containing the pair `(i, j)`, divided by the total weight `Z` of all structures. For nonnegative weights `Z ≥ 1` (the empty structure has weight `1`), so the denominator is positive; for Boltzmann weights this is the probability of `(i, j)` under the Boltzmann distribution on structures.

results.title: McCaskill's base-pair probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For a candidate pair `(i, j)`, `P(i, j) = outside(i, j) · w(i, j) · inside(i + 1, j) / inside(0, n)`.

results.title: Total structure weight is at least one
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For nonnegative weights the total weight of all structures is at least `1`, the weight of the empty structure; so the denominator of `pairProb` is positive.

results.title: Nonnegativity of base-pair probabilities
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: Base-pair probabilities are nonnegative for nonnegative weights.

results.title: Each base pairs at most once
results.caption: Theorem
results.summary: For nonnegative weights, the probabilities that base `i` pairs with some later base `j` or some earlier base `j` sum to at most `1` (`∑_j (P(i, j) + P(j, i)) ≤ 1`).
